case_text_full:
Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with painless vaginal bleeding that began earlier in the day. She is at 36 weeks gestation in her 3rd pregnancy; she has had one previous full-term delivery and one spontaneous 1st-trimester abortion. She noticed a small amount of brown discharge on the toilet paper while wiping this morning. Later in the day, she noticed dark red blood on her underwear and decided to come to the emergency department. She denies fluid discharge, abdominal pain, or cramping, and she is feeling usual fetal movement. She has had no abdominal trauma. She has received all routine prenatal care and reports that everything has been normal until now.

Review of Systems:
General: She reports appropriate weight gain this pregnancy. She has felt fatigued for the past few weeks but has been able to do her normal duties at work. No recent injuries or falls.

Skin: No rash or easy bruising or bleeding.

HEENT: No bleeding from nose or gums.

Pulmonary: No shortness of breath.

Cardiovascular: No palpitations; no chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or cramping.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, urgency or frequency.

Musculoskeletal: No swelling or pain in extremities or joints.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Obstetric: G3P1011 No other episodes of vaginal bleeding during this pregnancy. Had routine ultrasonography at 20 weeks which she was told was normal. She is unsure of her Rh status.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Asthma with no recent exacerbations. No history of bleeding disorder.

Surgical history: None

Obstetric history: Menarche at age 12 years. One first-trimester miscarriage 6 years prior. One uncomplicated full-term vaginal delivery of a healthy 7.5-pound female infant 3 years prior. Patient has received all her prenatal care at another facility and her records are unavailable.

Medications: Prenatal vitamin, albuterol as needed.

Allergies: None

Family history: Noncontributory

Social history: Smokes 2 cigarettes a day, down from half a pack a day at the beginning of pregnancy. She denies alcohol and drug use. She lives at home with her fiancé and her daughter. She is employed as a security guard at a local college.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Appears well and in no distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 88 beats/min
BP: 118/64 mm Hg
Respirations: 20/min

Skin: No petechiae, ecchymoses, or other lesions.

HEENT: No scleral icterus or signs of bleeding.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear

Cardiovascular: Mild tachycardia; regular rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.

Gastrointestinal: Gravid abdomen, fundal height normal for dates. Uterus normal tone, nontender.

Genitourinary: Scant dried brown blood at the introitus. On speculum exam, a few milliliters of dark red blood are present in the vaginal vault. The cervix appears approximately 1-cm dilated, no active bleeding. Bimanual examination not done.

Test Results:
External fetal monitoring and tocometry: Few irregular contractions and a reactive fetal heart rate tracing at 150 beats/minute.


Ultrasonography: Cephalic presenting fetus and a fundal placenta with its margins clear of the region of the cervical os. Amniotic fluid index 15.7 cm (normal range: 8-18 cm)


Blood Tests:

Test (units) Results Results (SI Units)
Hemoglobin 10.9 gm/dL (109 g/L)
Platelets 238,000/mcL (238 x 109/L)
Type and screen A+ 
Kleihauer-Betke test Negative 
Fibrinogen 402 mg/dL (11.8 micromol/L), within normal range
PT/PTT Normal

The patient remains in the emergency department awaiting further evaluation. One hour later you are called to reassess the patient who has begun complaining of irregular cramping and contractions that are getting slightly stronger.


Her fetal monitor now shows the following:

Uterine irritability, few contractions with overall minimal variability and periods of absent variability and recurrent late decelerations.


On the bed pad there is approximately 50 cc bright-red blood.


Repeat vital signs show:

Temperature: 37.2 C
Pulse: 98/min
BP: 127/81 mm Hg
Respirations: 18/min


With a known fundal placental location, you do an internal exam that shows she is 3-cm dilated with cervix 50% effaced and fetal station -3 and there is scanty visible bleeding from the cervix.
participant_role_description__deepseekv4: Provides anesthetic care for emergent cesarean delivery in women with obstetric hemorrhage and evolving coagulopathy. Selects general versus neuraxial anesthesia based on maternal hemodynamic stability, platelet count, and fibrinogen level, favoring rapid sequence general anesthesia when shock or consumptive coagulopathy makes a regional technique unsafe. Secures large-bore intravenous access, directs massive transfusion and vasopressor support, and anticipates further blood loss and disseminated intravascular coagulation during and after delivery.
participant_role_description__gpt120b_dy: Manages medical complications arising during pregnancy while monitoring maternal and fetal wellbeing. Recognizes ascending urinary tract infection as a leading cause of antepartum hospitalization and anticipates its complications, including preterm contractions, sepsis, and acute respiratory distress. Assesses fetal heart rate and uterine activity, selects medications and imaging that are safe at the given gestational age, and decides on admission for intravenous therapy. Arranges repeat urine culture and suppressive prophylaxis for the remainder of gestation.
participant_role_description__qwen_dynam: Manages high-risk obstetric complications including antepartum hemorrhage in women with hypertensive disease and a prior abruption. Recognizes a tender, woody, contracted uterus with dark vaginal bleeding and a non-reassuring fetal heart tracing showing tachycardia, absent variability, and repetitive late decelerations as placental abruption rather than placenta previa or uterine rupture. Directs immediate maternal stabilization, coordinates blood product replacement, and calls for emergent cesarean delivery when fetal status is deteriorating and maternal bleeding threatens hemodynamic collapse.

winner_protocol:
Age: 32  
Sex: Female  

Complaint: Painless vaginal bleeding that progressed from brown spotting to dark‑red/bright‑red blood, new uterine irritability with strengthening contractions, recurrent late decelerations on fetal monitoring, and progressive cervical change (now 3 cm dilated, 50 % effaced) at 36 weeks gestation.  

Analysis:  
- The combination of painless third‑trimester bleeding, a fundal placenta away from the cervical os, sudden onset uterine irritability, and a Category III fetal heart‑rate pattern (recurrent late decelerations with minimal/absent variability) is classic for acute placental abruption with concealed hemorrhage.  
- Maternal vitals remain stable but tachycardia (HR 98) and increasing bleeding (≈50 cc bright red) indicate ongoing hemorrhage.  
- Differential diagnoses considered: placenta previa, vasa previa, cervical lesions, uterine rupture, and infection.  
  * Placenta previa is unlikely because ultrasound shows a fundal placenta clear of the os; no evidence of marginal sinus bleed on repeat imaging.  
  * Vasa previa would present with fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture, which is absent.  
  * Uterine rupture is improbable (no prior uterine surgery, no severe abdominal pain, uterus non‑tender).  
  * Infection (chorioamnionitis) is not suggested by maternal fever or leukocytosis.  
- Therefore, acute placental abruption is the most probable diagnosis and explains both maternal bleeding and fetal compromise.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Repeat bedside obstetric ultrasound (transabdominal ± transvaginal) to reassess placental location and look for retro‑placental clot.  
- Complete blood count with differential.  
- Coagulation profile: PT, PTT, fibrinogen.  
- Type and screen, Rh typing, and Kleihauer‑Betke test if Rh‑negative.  
- Arterial or venous blood gas (if available) to assess maternal/fetal acid‑base status.  
- Continuous electronic fetal monitoring (already in place).  

Conclusion: Acute placental abruption with concealed hemorrhage causing fetal hypoxia and progressive maternal bleeding at 36 weeks gestation, necessitating immediate delivery.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Activate obstetric emergency** – notify maternal‑fetal medicine, obstetric anesthesia, neonatology, and blood bank.  
2. **Maternal stabilization** – place patient in left lateral decubitus, administer supplemental O₂, obtain two large‑bore (16‑18 G) IV lines, begin crystalloid bolus.  
3. **Laboratory preparation** – draw blood for CBC, coagulation panel, type & screen, Rh typing; if Rh‑negative, give Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) within 72 h of any fetomaternal hemorrhage.  
4. **Massive transfusion protocol** – have packed RBCs, plasma, platelets (1:1:1 ratio) and cryoprecipitate ready; monitor fibrinogen and replace if <200 mg/dL; consider tranexamic acid 1 g IV.  
5. **Anesthetic plan** – proceed with rapid‑sequence induction general anesthesia (cricoid pressure, pre‑oxygenation, aspiration prophylaxis with non‑particulate antacid, H₂‑blocker, metoclopramide). Avoid neuraxial techniques due to potential coagulopathy. Prepare difficult‑airway algorithm (pregnancy‑related airway edema).  
6. **Surgical management** – emergent cesarean delivery (Category III fetal tracing, cervical dilation 3 cm, active bleeding).  
7. **Post‑delivery uterine management** – administer uterotonics (oxytocin infusion, methylergonovine, carboprost as needed), assess uterine tone, consider uterine massage or surgical hemostasis if atony persists.  
8. **Cell salvage** – may be employed with leukocyte filtration if significant blood loss anticipated, acknowledging theoretical amniotic fluid embolism risk.  
9. **Neonatal care** – ensure neonatal team present; anticipate possible respiratory support despite near‑term gestation.  
10. **Post‑operative monitoring** – serial CBC, coagulation studies, fibrinogen; watch for postpartum hemorrhage and disseminated intravascular coagulation.  
11. **Address comorbidities** –  
    - **Smoking**: provide cessation counseling and nicotine‑replacement options.  
    - **Asthma**: continue maintenance inhalers; avoid histamine‑releasing agents intra‑operatively; monitor respiratory status.  
    - **Anemia**: baseline Hb 10.9 g/dL; transfuse if Hb < 8 g/dL or symptomatic.  
12. **Medication considerations** – corticosteroids are not indicated at 36 weeks (lung maturity near term).  
13. **Pathology** – send placenta and membranes for histopathologic examination.  

Notes:  
- Placenta previa was considered but excluded by imaging; thus management follows abruptio protocol.  
- Rh status remains unknown; ensure Rh immunoglobulin administration if indicated.  
- No tocolysis is given because fetal distress is present.  
- Ensure documentation of all interventions and counseling provided.

  [2] +10 pts — The protocol mandates emergent cesarean delivery due to Category III fetal tracing with suspected abruption and activates labor and delivery, anesthesia, neonatology, and blood bank immediately.
  [3] +9 pts — The protocol correctly identifies the fetal heart rate tracing as Category III due to minimal/absent variability with recurrent late decelerations and emphasizes that the diagnosis of abruption is clinical despite ultrasound being used to exclude placenta previa.
  [4] +9 pts — The protocol includes establishing two large-bore IV lines, ordering type and screen with coagulation studies including fibrinogen, preparing packed RBCs, plasma, platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio, and monitoring fibrinogen and coagulation post-delivery to watch for DIC, thus fulfilling the massive transfusion protocol preparation.
  [5] +8 pts — The protocol explicitly recommends maternal stabilization including left lateral decubitus positioning, supplemental oxygen, two large-bore IV lines with crystalloid bolus, and continuous electronic fetal monitoring, fulfilling the criterion.
  [6] +8 pts — The protocol explicitly differentiates placental abruption from placenta previa, vasa previa, uterine rupture, and infection, and notes that painless bleeding can occur in abruption despite classic teaching of painful bleeding.
  [7] +7 pts — The protocol includes urgent Rh typing and administration of Rh immunoglobulin if Rh-negative, with Kleihauer-Betke test performed and consideration for repeat testing.
  [8] +7 pts — The protocol explicitly addresses smoking as a risk factor and includes counseling on smoking cessation, fulfilling the criterion.
  [9] +6 pts — The protocol explicitly states that corticosteroids are not indicated at 36 weeks due to near-term lung maturity and the emergent need for delivery, satisfying the criterion.

Vignette: A 35-year-old man who is an avid hiker in Connecticut presents with a 5-day history of an expanding red rash on his right thigh that he noticed after a weekend camping trip two weeks ago. He recalls removing an engorged tick from his thigh. He now reports fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias in his knees and wrists, and low-grade fever. He denies neck stiffness, facial weakness, chest pain, or palpitations. On examination, temperature is 99.6°F. There is a 12 cm annular erythematous plaque on the right anterior thigh with central clearing, consistent with erythema migrans. There are no secondary skin lesions. Joints are nontender without effusion. Neurological examination is nonfocal. Heart rate is regular at 74 with no murmurs. There is no cervical rigidity.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Identifies early localized Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) based on classic erythema migrans (>5 cm annular lesion with central clearing) in an endemic area (Connecticut) with tick attachment history and constitutional symptoms.

[2]
points: 9
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Recommends empiric oral doxycycline 100 mg BID for 10-14 days as first-line therapy for early Lyme disease in an adult (no signs of CNS, cardiac, or arthritis involvement).

[3]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Notes that serologic testing is NOT recommended in early localized disease with classic EM in an endemic area-treatment is clinical, and early serology has poor sensitivity (often negative in the first 2-4 weeks).

[4]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Lists red flags requiring more aggressive workup/care: cranial nerve palsy (facial), meningitis signs (severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia), heart block (chest pain, palpitations, syncope, dyspnea), or large joint arthritis.

[5]
points: 7

criterion:
Differentiates EM from southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI), tinea corporis, cellulitis, granuloma annulare, contact dermatitis, and erythema annulare centrifugum based on size, evolution, and exposure.

[6]
points: 7
tags: ['axis:completeness']

Mentions alternative antibiotics for doxycycline contraindications: amoxicillin or cefuroxime (e.g., pregnancy, lactation if avoiding doxy, children-though doxy is now considered safe short-course in children).

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']

Discusses Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction possibility within 24 hours of starting therapy and counsels patient on expected resolution timeline (rash fades within days; constitutional symptoms within 1-2 weeks).

Provides clear tick-bite prevention counseling: protective clothing, DEET/picaridin/permethrin, daily tick checks, prompt removal of attached ticks, and outdoor activity precautions for future hikes.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[5]
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man who is an avid hiker in Connecticut presents with a 5-day history of an expanding red rash on his right thigh that he noticed after a weekend camping trip two weeks ago. He recalls removing an engorged tick from his thigh. He now reports fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias in his knees and wrists, and low-grade fever. He denies neck stiffness, facial weakness, chest pain, or palpitations. On examination, temperature is 99.6°F. There is a 12 cm annular erythematous plaque on the right anterior thigh with central clearing, consistent with erythema migrans. There are no secondary skin lesions. Joints are nontender without effusion. Neurological examination is nonfocal. Heart rate is regular at 74 with no murmurs. There is no cervical rigidity.

Age: 35  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: 12 cm erythema migrans on the right thigh with central clearing, fatigue, arthralgias, headache, and low‑grade fever (99.6 °F) two weeks after tick removal.  

Analysis:  
- The annular rash with central clearing (erythema migrans) in a patient with a recent tick bite in an endemic area (Connecticut) is pathognomonic for early localized Lyme disease.  
- Systemic symptoms (fatigue, arthralgias, headache, low‑grade fever) are typical early manifestations.  
- Vital signs are stable; there is no neurologic (e.g., facial palsy, meningitis) or cardiac involvement (e.g., AV block, palpitations), supporting a non‑disseminated stage.  
- Differential diagnoses to consider include other tick‑borne illnesses (anaplasmosis, babesiosis, STARI), cellulitis, fungal infection (tinea corporis), and erythema multiforme; however, the characteristic appearance and epidemiology make Lyme disease the most likely.  
- Red‑flag features that would require urgent reassessment are new neurologic deficits, cardiac symptoms, high fever (>101 °F), rapidly expanding or necrotic rash, or signs of sepsis.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: Early localized Lyme disease (erythema migrans) without evidence of dissemination.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  

Recommendations:  
1. **Antibiotic therapy** – Start oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10–14 days (extend to 21 days if co‑infection is suspected).  
   - If doxycycline is contraindicated (pregnancy, age < 8 years, tetracycline allergy, severe renal/hepatic impairment), prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily for the same duration.  
2. **Counseling** –  
   - Explain that symptoms may persist for several weeks despite appropriate therapy.  
   - Advise completion of the full antibiotic course.  
   - Warn about a possible Jarisch‑Herxheimer‑type reaction (fever, chills, myalgias) within the first 24 hours of treatment; this is self‑limited.  
   - Instruct the patient to seek immediate care if new neurologic signs (e.g., facial weakness, severe headache with neck stiffness), cardiac symptoms (palpitations, syncope), high fever, or a rapidly changing rash develop.  
   - Provide tick‑prevention education: proper removal technique, use of EPA‑registered repellents (e.g., DEET, picaridin), wearing long sleeves/pants, and performing full‑body tick checks after outdoor activities.  
3. **Follow‑up** – Arrange an outpatient visit in 2–3 weeks to assess rash resolution and systemic symptom improvement.  
4. **Consider co‑infection** – If the patient develops fever >101 °F, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, or other atypical findings, obtain baseline CBC and liver function tests and consider serologic testing for Anaplasma and Babesia.  
5. **Documentation** – Record the estimated duration of tick attachment (if known) and note that >36 hours increases transmission risk.  
6. **Long‑term monitoring** – Educate about post‑treatment Lyme disease syndrome; persistent fatigue or joint pain beyond the treatment course should be evaluated but does not require additional antibiotics without evidence of active infection.  

Notes: None

Age: 6 weeks  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Inconsolable crying for 2–3 hours each evening, with the infant drawing up his knees; feeding well and weight gain normal (50th percentile).  

Analysis: The infant meets classic Wessel criteria for infantile colic: age < 3 months, paroxysmal crying > 3 hours/day, > 3 days/week, occurring in the evening, with normal growth and no systemic signs. The physical exam is reported as normal and there are no red‑flag features (fever, vomiting, bloody stools, poor feeding, lethargy, dehydration, abdominal distension, abnormal neurologic findings). These findings strongly support a diagnosis of infantile colic and make serious organic pathology unlikely. Relevant differentials to keep in mind—though not suggested by the current history—include gastro‑esophageal reflux disease, cow‑milk protein allergy, constipation, otitis media, urinary‑tract infection, intussusception, malrotation/volvulus, sepsis, and hair‑tourniquet syndrome. A focused history (feeding type, family atopy, sleep patterns, environmental factors) and a thorough newborn exam (including scalp, digits, genitalia, hips) are useful to exclude these conditions.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: Infantile colic (benign infantile dysphoria).  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations:  
1. **Parental reassurance** – explain that colic is self‑limited, typically resolves by 3–4 months of age.  
2. **Non‑pharmacologic soothing** – swaddling, rocking, white‑noise, infant‑wearing, paced feeding, gentle motion (e.g., car ride or swing).  
3. **Assess feeding type** – ask whether the infant is breast‑fed or formula‑fed.  
   - If formula‑fed, consider a trial of a hypoallergenic (e.g., extensively hydrolyzed) formula for 1–2 weeks.  
   - If breast‑fed and cow‑milk protein allergy is suspected, discuss a maternal dairy‑free diet.  
4. **Probiotic trial** – a short course of Lactobacillus reuteri (per product dosing) may be offered; counsel that evidence is mixed.  
5. **Physical exam checklist** – during the visit, specifically examine scalp, digits, genitalia, and hips to rule out hair‑tourniquet or congenital anomalies.  
6. **Cry‑log** – encourage caregivers to record crying episodes, duration, and any attempted soothing measures to identify possible patterns or triggers.  
7. **Caregiver support** – screen for parental stress, postpartum depression, and risk of shaken‑baby syndrome; provide resources (e.g., mental‑health hotlines, support groups, respite services).  
8. **Environmental review** – ask about infant sleep duration, nighttime awakenings, and household factors (noise, lighting, temperature) that might affect irritability.  
9. **Follow‑up** – schedule routine well‑child visit in 2–4 weeks. Advise caregivers to return sooner if any red‑flag symptoms develop (fever, vomiting, bloody stools, poor feeding, lethargy, persistent inconsolable crying despite soothing, abdominal distension, signs of dehydration).  

Notes: None

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Age: 27  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 3‑day history of cough, mild shortness of breath, wheezing, and lack of response to usual rescue inhalers following a recent cold.  

Analysis:  
The patient has a known history of asthma and presents with a recent upper‑respiratory viral infection, cough, wheeze, and dyspnea that have not improved with home short‑acting β₂‑agonist (SABA) therapy. These findings are classic for an acute asthma exacerbation precipitated by a viral trigger. The absence of red‑flag signs (no fever, hypoxia, cyanosis, chest pain, altered mental status, or accessory‑muscle use) makes a life‑threatening mimic (e.g., pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, anaphylaxis) less likely, but they must still be considered and excluded. Differential diagnoses to keep in mind include: viral bronchitis, bacterial pneumonia, COVID‑19 infection, upper airway cough syndrome (post‑nasal drip), gastro‑esophageal reflux disease, poor inhaler technique, drug‑induced cough, and allergic rhinitis/sinusitis.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Pulse oximetry (room‑air SpO₂)  
- Peak expiratory flow (PEF) measurement or handheld spirometry (pre‑ and post‑bronchodilator if available)  
- Rapid COVID‑19 antigen or PCR test (given recent URI)  
- Pregnancy test (urine β‑hCG) before systemic corticosteroid administration (patient is of child‑bearing age)  
- Chest radiograph **if** fever, focal auscultatory findings, or concern for pneumonia/complication arises  
- Assessment of inhaler technique (visual inspection and demonstration)  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with a mild‑to‑moderate acute asthma exacerbation triggered by a recent viral upper‑respiratory infection, without current danger signs. Non‑emergent, prompt outpatient evaluation is appropriate.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Urgent outpatient/urgent‑care visit** within the next 24 hours for objective assessment (SpO₂, PEF) and initiation of therapy.  
2. **Acute management** at the visit:  
   - Administer SABA (albuterol MDI with spacer or nebulizer) repeatedly as needed.  
   - Start oral systemic corticosteroid (e.g., prednisone 40 mg daily ×5 days) **after** confirming a negative pregnancy test or discussing risks/benefits if pregnancy cannot be excluded.  
   - Provide supplemental oxygen if SpO₂ < 92 % on room air.  
3. **Review and correct inhaler technique**; demonstrate proper MDI/spacer use or consider switching to a dry‑powder inhaler if technique remains problematic.  
4. **Ensure controller therapy**: verify that a low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) is prescribed and taken regularly; if not, initiate or step‑up the ICS regimen.  
5. **Vaccination review**: assess and update influenza, COVID‑19, and pneumococcal vaccinations as indicated.  
6. **Identify and address comorbidities/triggers**:  
   - Ask about allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, GERD symptoms, smoking/vaping, and environmental allergens; treat or refer as appropriate.  
   - Document recent use of systemic steroids or antibiotics for the preceding cold.  
7. **Social determinants**: evaluate medication access, insurance coverage, and ability to attend follow‑up; arrange pharmacy assistance or community resources if needed.  
8. **COVID‑19 testing**: perform rapid antigen or PCR test now; if positive, follow local infectious‑disease guidance while continuing asthma management.  
9. **Follow‑up plan**:  
   - Re‑evaluate in 48–72 hours (telehealth or in‑person) to assess symptom improvement and repeat PEF.  
   - Schedule spirometry in 1–2 weeks to confirm baseline lung function and adjust long‑term therapy.

winner_protocol:
Age: 26  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Dysuria with urgency and increased frequency for 2 days; sexually active.  

Analysis: The patient’s acute onset of dysuria, urinary urgency, and frequency without systemic symptoms strongly suggests uncomplicated acute cystitis, the most common lower urinary tract infection in young women. The absence of fever, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, gross hematuria, or hemodynamic instability makes upper‑tract involvement (pyelonephritis) or sepsis unlikely. Sexual activity raises the possibility of STI‑related urethritis (chlamydia, gonorrhea) and co‑existing vaginitis, which must be considered in the differential. Key differentials include:  
- Uncomplicated acute cystitis (primary working diagnosis)  
- STI‑related urethritis (chlamydial or gonococcal)  
- Vaginitis (candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis)  
- Early pyelonephritis (red‑flag symptoms absent)  
- Interstitial cystitis, urolithiasis, bladder foreign body (less likely).  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Mid‑stream clean‑catch urine sample for dipstick, microscopy, and culture  
- Urine pregnancy test (point‑of‑care)  
- NAAT for **Chlamydia trachomatis** and **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** (urine or vaginal swab)  
- Focused pelvic examination (visual inspection, speculum, bimanual) if vaginal discharge, irritation, or lesions are reported  
- Consider HIV serology and syphilis testing based on individual risk factors (as part of broader sexual‑health assessment)  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated acute cystitis in a non‑pregnant, sexually active young woman, without red‑flag features. STI screening and pregnancy testing are essential adjuncts to guide safe antimicrobial selection.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  

Recommendations:  
1. **Empiric antimicrobial therapy** – Start nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO twice daily for 5 days (first‑line).  
   - If local **E. coli** resistance to nitrofurantoin is high or patient is allergic, use TMP‑SMX 160/800 mg PO BID for 3 days provided local resistance <20 %.  
   - Reserve fluoroquinolones for documented resistance or complications.  
   - If clinical suspicion for urethritis is high (e.g., urethral discharge, recent STI exposure), add a single dose of ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g PO.  

2. **Pregnancy considerations** – Perform urine pregnancy test now.  
   - If positive and patient is in the third trimester, avoid nitrofurantoin; use amoxicillin or cephalexin instead and involve obstetrics.  

3. **Diagnostic work‑up** – Obtain urine studies and STI NAAT as listed above before or at the time of prescribing antibiotics. Adjust therapy according to urine culture sensitivities if the culture returns resistant organisms or if symptoms persist beyond 48–72 hours.  

4. **Counseling & education** –  
   - Complete the full antibiotic course.  
   - Increase oral fluid intake (≥2 L/day) to aid bacterial clearance.  
   - Avoid bladder irritants (caffeine, alcohol, acidic or spicy foods) while symptomatic.  
   - Monitor for red‑flag signs (fever ≥38 °C, flank pain, worsening dysuria, vomiting) and seek care promptly if they develop.  
   - Return for reassessment in 48–72 hours if no improvement.  
   - Discuss safe‑sex practices, condom use, and the importance of partner notification/treatment if an STI is confirmed.  
   - Review contraceptive method; advise against spermicidal agents that increase UTI risk.  

5. **Follow‑up & referral** –  
   - Primary care or OB‑GYN can manage initially.  
   - Refer to urology for recurrent (≥3 episodes/year) or complicated UTIs, or if anatomic abnormalities are suspected.  
   - Refer to infectious disease if resistant pathogen identified or confirmed STI requiring specialized management.  
   - Involve obstetrics promptly if pregnancy is confirmed.  

Notes: None.

- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. - the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

winner_protocol:
Age: 2 months  
Sex: Male  

Complaint: Yellowish greasy scales on the scalp for 2 weeks; no erythema, oozing, or involvement of face/diaper area; infant feeding and weight gain are normal.  

Analysis: The infant presents with classic “cradle cap” – greasy, yellow‑white scales confined to the scalp of a well‑appearing 2‑month‑old without inflammation or systemic signs. This presentation strongly supports infantile seborrheic dermatitis. Supporting facts:  
- Age < 3 months, typical onset.  
- Greasy, non‑erythematous scaling limited to scalp.  
- No pain, fever, or growth concerns.  
- Absence of facial or diaper involvement (still compatible, as seborrheic sites may appear later).  

Key differentials considered: atopic dermatitis, infantile psoriasis, tinea capitis, bacterial impetigo/contact dermatitis, and rare entities such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Each alternative is less likely because they usually present with erythema, pruritus, alopecia, crusting, systemic symptoms, or a different distribution.  

Additional considerations from the expert discussion:  
- No gender predilection.  
- Pathogenesis involves Malassezia yeast and residual maternal hormones (does not change management).  
- Family history of atopic dermatitis or psoriasis may broaden differentials but is not present here.  
- Recent antibiotic or immunosuppressive exposure could predispose to secondary infection; none reported.  
- Harsh hair products, fragrances, or detergents can aggravate irritation – advise avoidance.  
- Examination of other typical seborrheic sites (nasolabial folds, trunk) is useful to confirm the diagnosis.  
- Parental anxiety about appearance warrants reassurance and education.  
- Rare refractory cases may be linked to immunodeficiency or metabolic disorders; unlikely in this well‑appearing infant.  
- Low‑potency topical steroids or antifungals are optional for refractory scaling (not first‑line).  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: Infantile seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap) – a benign, self‑limited condition that does not require emergent care or diagnostic testing.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Scale softening** – Apply a small amount of mineral oil, baby oil, or a fragrance‑free emollient to the scalp; leave for 5–10 minutes.  
2. **Mechanical removal** – Gently brush or comb with a soft brush/fine‑toothed comb to lift softened scales.  
3. **Cleansing** – Wash the scalp 2–3 times per week with a mild, fragrance‑free baby shampoo; rinse thoroughly.  
4. **Escalation (if scaling persists after 2 weeks)** – Use a medicated shampoo (ketoconazole 1 % or selenium sulfide 2.5 %) once or twice weekly for up to 2 weeks.  
5. **Refractory cases** – Consider a short course of low‑potency topical steroid (e.g., 1 % hydrocortisone) or antifungal (e.g., ketoconazole cream) applied to inflamed areas only; avoid prolonged use.  
6. **Red‑flag monitoring** – Seek re‑evaluation if any of the following appear: new erythema, oozing, crusting, fever, irritability, poor feeding/weight loss, rapid spread to face or diaper area, or lack of improvement after 2 weeks of proper care.  
7. **Parental education** – Reassure that the condition is common and self‑limited, typically resolving by 6–12 months. Advise avoidance of harsh hair products, fragrances, or detergents.  
8. **Additional assessment** – Review family skin‑disease history, recent antibiotic exposure, and examine other seborrheic sites (nasolabial folds, trunk). Confirm that developmental milestones and immunizations are up to date.  
9. **Follow‑up** – Routine well‑child visit is sufficient unless red‑flag signs develop.  

Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

case_text_full:
Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents to her obstetrician's office with a 2-day history of high fever, body aches, headache, sore throat, and a dry nonproductive cough. She reports mild rhinorrhea and fatigue. She did not receive the influenza vaccine this season. Vital signs show temperature 101.8°F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The fundal height is consistent with gestational age and fetal heart tones are reassuring at 145 bpm. Rapid influenza antigen test is positive for influenza A. She has no signs of respiratory distress or dehydration.

Age: 30  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Fever (101.8 °F) with myalgias, headache, sore throat, dry cough; positive influenza A test at 28 weeks gestation.  

Analysis: The patient presents with an acute influenza A infection confirmed by rapid testing. Vital signs are stable (SpO₂ 97% on room air) and fetal heart tones are reassuring, indicating mild current severity. Pregnancy (third trimester) and lack of prior influenza vaccination increase the risk for rapid maternal decompensation, secondary bacterial infection, and adverse fetal outcomes. Differential diagnoses include other viral respiratory infections (COVID‑19, RSV, parainfluenza), bacterial pneumonia, urinary‑tract infection/pyelonephritis, and atypical infections (e.g., leptospirosis, Q fever). These are considered because co‑infection can occur and would alter management if the clinical course worsens.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- CBC with differential  
- Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP)  
- CRP or procalcitonin  
- Urinalysis and urine culture  
- SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR (or rapid antigen)  
- Fetal assessment: non‑stress test (NST) or biophysical profile (BPP)  
- Chest radiograph with abdominal shielding **only if** respiratory status deteriorates or sepsis is suspected  
- Blood cultures **if** fever >39.5 °C or other sepsis signs develop  

Conclusion: Acute influenza A infection in a 28‑week pregnant woman, currently mild in severity but high‑risk due to gestational physiologic changes and lack of vaccination.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Antiviral therapy:** Start oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days immediately (benefit persists beyond 48 h in pregnancy). Adjust dose to 75 mg once daily if creatinine clearance <30 mL/min.  
2. **Symptomatic care:** Acetaminophen 650 mg q6‑8 h PRN for fever/pain; encourage aggressive oral hydration and rest. Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester.  
3. **Isolation precautions:** Advise the patient to stay home, limit contact with others, wear a mask when around people, and practice hand hygiene. Clinic staff should use standard droplet precautions if in‑person evaluation is needed.  
4. **Baseline investigations:** Obtain the labs and fetal testing listed above today to assess for co‑infection, organ function, and fetal well‑being.  
5. **Outpatient monitoring:**  
   - Same‑day or next‑day obstetric follow‑up (in‑person or telehealth).  
   - Telephone/telehealth check‑in at 24‑48 h after initiating therapy.  
   - Provide written red‑flag instructions (see below).  
6. **Red‑flag criteria (prompt return or admission):**  
   - SpO₂ < 94 % on room air or increasing dyspnea/tachypnea.  
   - Fever > 39.5 °C or persistent fever > 48 h.  
   - Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia out of proportion to fever).  
   - Altered mental status.  
   - New productive cough, sputum, or signs of bacterial infection.  
   - Fetal non‑reassuring heart rate patterns, decreased fetal movements, or onset of pre‑term labor.  
7. **Social assessment:** Verify the patient’s ability to self‑monitor temperature, maintain hydration/oral intake, and access urgent care if needed. Arrange support (family, home health) if barriers exist; consider admission if safe outpatient monitoring cannot be ensured.  
8. **Preventive counseling:**  
   - Discuss influenza vaccination for future pregnancies and postpartum (safe and recommended).  
   - Recommend vaccination of all household contacts.  
   - Reinforce hand hygiene, mask use, and respiratory etiquette during the flu season.  
   - Explain the importance of early presentation for any worsening symptoms.  

Notes: None.

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old male college student presents with a painful sore inside his mouth for the past 2 days. He is in the middle of final examinations and reports increased stress and poor sleep. He denies fever, multiple ulcers, genital sores, or joint pain. He has no history of inflammatory bowel disease. On examination, a single shallow oval ulcer approximately 5 mm in diameter is visible on the buccal mucosa of the left cheek. It has a white-yellowish base with an erythematous halo. The remainder of the oral exam is unremarkable. There is no lymphadenopathy.

winner_protocol:
Age: 22  
Sex: Male  

Complaint: Painful solitary ulcer on the right buccal mucosa for 2 days, white base with erythematous halo; occurring during a period of stress, no fever or systemic symptoms.  

Analysis: The lesion’s classic appearance (small, painful ulcer with a white/gray fibrinous base surrounded by an erythematous halo) on non‑keratinised buccal mucosa in a young adult, together with a known stress trigger and absence of systemic signs, strongly supports a diagnosis of **minor recurrent aphthous ulcer (minor aphthous stomatitis)**.  

Key supporting facts:  
- Solitary ulcer, <1 cm, painful.  
- White base, erythematous halo.  
- Duration < 1 week.  
- No fever, no multiple lesions, no lymphadenopathy.  
- Stress as precipitating factor.  

Relevant differentials (to keep in mind, especially if atypical features develop):  
1. Traumatic ulcer (cheek biting, sharp tooth or restoration).  
2. Herpes simplex virus ulcer (primary or recurrent).  
3. Major or herpetiform aphthous ulcer.  
4. Behçet’s disease.  
5. Early neoplastic lesion (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma).  
6. Infectious ulcers – syphilis (primary chancre) and oral tuberculosis (rare).  

Red‑flag features that would prompt urgent re‑evaluation: ulcer persisting >2 weeks, induration or irregular borders, multiple/rapidly spreading lesions, systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy), dysphagia/odynophagia, immunosuppression, or prior history of oral cancer.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with a **minor recurrent aphthous ulcer**, a benign, self‑limited condition that does not require emergency care and can be managed with self‑care measures.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations:  
1. **Symptomatic therapy** – apply a topical anesthetic (e.g., benzocaine or lidocaine gel) 2–3 times daily for pain relief.  
2. **Anti‑inflammatory/topical steroid** – apply triamcinolone acetonide 0.1 % paste (or clobetasol 0.05 % paste) to the ulcer 2–3 times daily to reduce inflammation and hasten healing.  
3. **Mouth rinse** – use chlorhexidine 0.12 % or a “magic mouthwash” (e.g., diphenhydramine + hydrocortisone + nystatin) 2–3 times daily.  
4. **Barrier protection** – consider a protective paste (e.g., sucralfate suspension or a commercial barrier gel) to shield the ulcer from mechanical irritation.  
5. **Oral hygiene & irritant avoidance** – advise gentle brushing, avoidance of spicy, acidic, or rough foods, and refrain from cheek‑biting.  
6. **Stress management** – encourage stress‑reduction techniques (e.g., relaxation exercises, adequate sleep, counseling if needed).  
7. **Nutrition & deficiency screening** – if ulcers become recurrent, obtain CBC, iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate levels; otherwise, no labs are needed now.  
8. **Follow‑up criteria** – re‑evaluate if the ulcer persists beyond 2 weeks, enlarges, becomes indurated, new lesions appear, or systemic symptoms develop. At that point, consider biopsy and referral to oral medicine, ENT, dermatology, or oncology as appropriate.  

Notes: None.

Vignette: A 68-year-old male farmer presents with a slowly growing lesion on his nose that he first noticed approximately 8 months ago. The lesion has gradually enlarged and occasionally bleeds when he washes his face but heals over. He has extensive sun exposure from decades of outdoor work and a history of multiple sunburns in his youth. He has never had skin cancer before. On examination, there is a 1.2 cm pearly, dome-shaped nodule on the left ala of the nose with a rolled border and central depression. Multiple telangiectasias are visible on the surface. The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.
